label: Amendment 1
t: Disabled veteran's spouse can move tax exemption once
what: Lets the surviving spouse of a veteran with a service-connected disability, who already receives the extra property-tax exemption, transfer it one time to a new home. The transferred exemption is capped at the amount claimed on the prior home. Applies from tax year 2027.
y: A qualifying surviving spouse who moves can carry the exemption to the new home once.
n: The surviving spouse keeps the exemption only while owning and living in the original home.
fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office: revenue impact not expected to be significant. 229 surviving spouses claimed the exemption in 2025 (about $1.6M of assessed value, roughly $168,000 a year in forgone local tax); how many would move in any year is indeterminable but expected to be low.
pro: Sen. Franklin Foil (R, sponsor); passed House 92-0 and Senate 36-0
con: No organised opposition; Pelican Institute (opposes new tax carve-outs)

label: Amendment 2
t: Keep right to restore prior maximum millage
what: Today, after a reassessment, a local taxing body that keeps its property-tax rate below the prior maximum permanently loses the ability to 'roll forward' to that maximum if it doesn't do so before the next reassessment. This lets it keep a lower rate without losing that ability until the authorized millage expires. Applies from tax year 2027.
y: Local taxing bodies can keep lower millage rates without forfeiting the right to raise them later to the prior voter-approved maximum.
n: The current 'use it or lose it' rule on rolling millage forward stays.
fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office: may result in forgone local property-tax revenue if taxing authorities defer rolling forward their millages; the extent is indeterminable and depends on each authority's decisions.
pro: Rep. Roger Wilder III (R, sponsor), Pelican Institute; passed House 95-0 and Senate 36-0

reasons.fiscal: The Legislative Fiscal Office says local governments may forgo some property-tax revenue by keeping lower rates longer, by an indeterminable amount.

label: Amendment 3
t: No post-conviction bail for aggravated crimes vs. minors
what: Adds to the constitution that a person convicted of an aggravated offense (as defined in state law) against a minor cannot be released on any bail after conviction, such as while awaiting sentencing or during an appeal.
y: People convicted of aggravated offenses against minors stay in custody after conviction with no bail.
n: Judges keep current discretion over post-conviction bail in these cases.
fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office: indeterminable increase in local sheriffs' jail costs from holding these offenders before transfer; no effect on revenues.
pro: Rep. Debbie Villio (R, sponsor), Attorney General Liz Murrill, Louisiana Fraternal Order of Police

label: Amendment 4
what: Changes the governor's term limit from two consecutive terms (after which a former governor can sit out a term and run again) to a lifetime limit: anyone who has served more than one and a half terms could never again be elected governor.
y: Governors are limited to two terms in their lifetime.
n: The limit stays at two consecutive terms, with no lifetime cap.
fiscal: No fiscal note identified; no material fiscal effect expected beyond minimal ballot costs.
pro: Rep. Michael Bayham (R, sponsor); passed largely along party lines (House 73-25, Senate 28-10)
con: Most Democratic legislators; Rep. Mark Wright (R) criticised it

label: Amendment 5
t: Let pension systems apply one-time money to any debt
what: The constitution requires at least 25% of nonrecurring (one-time) state revenue to go toward state retirement systems' unfunded liabilities, applied to the oldest liabilities first. This removes the oldest-first rule so systems can apply the money to any of their unfunded liabilities.
y: Retirement systems can apply one-time state money to whichever unfunded liability they choose.
n: One-time money must still pay down the oldest unfunded liability first.
fiscal: Legislative actuary: no change to any benefits; the impact of allowing systems to choose how to allocate the money is not actuarially measurable.
pro: Rep. Dixon McMakin (R, sponsor), Pelican Institute; passed House 87-0 and Senate 34-0

label: Amendment 6
t: Optional extra property-tax exemption for seniors 65+
what: Lets parishes and cities, if their own voters approve, give homeowners 65+ who qualify for the special assessment (income-based) freeze an extra exemption that rises with age: $6,000 of assessed value (=$60,000 market value) at 65-68 up to $30,000 (=$300,000 market value) at 81+. Taxing bodies must absorb the lost revenue rather than shift it to other taxpayers. Effective 2028.
y: Parishes and cities may offer (with local voter approval) an age-scaled extra homestead exemption for qualifying seniors.
n: No additional senior exemption beyond the existing $7,500 homestead exemption and the assessment freeze.
fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office: indeterminable but significant decrease in local property-tax revenue where adopted. Example: a 65-68-year-old with $6,000 extra exemption saves about $630/yr at the 105-mill statewide average; 184,329 seniors had the special assessment in 2025, so even $1,000 of extra exemption each would cost about $19.4M a year statewide. Possible indeterminate effects on state school (MFP) funding; assessor implementation costs may be significant statewide.
pro: Rep. Les Farnum (R, sponsor); passed House 93-0 and Senate 34-0
con: Pelican Institute (narrow carve-outs shift the tax burden)

reasons.fiscal: The Legislative Fiscal Office expects a significant (but indeterminable) loss of local property-tax revenue where parishes adopt it, which taxing bodies must absorb.

label: Amendment 7
t: Allow public money to replace lead service lines
what: Adds an exception to the constitution's ban on donating public funds so local governments may pay to identify, inventory, remove or replace drinking-water service lines made of or affected by lead and other materials covered by the EPA's 2024 Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, including the portion on customers' private property.
y: Local governments may spend public money on lead service-line work on private property.
n: Public money generally can't be used for the customer-owned portion of service lines.
fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office: may increase local spending to the extent political subdivisions use public funds for this work; no effect on revenues.
pro: Sen. Royce Duplessis (D, sponsor); passed Senate 32-4 and House 80-12

reasons.services: Allows local governments to fund removal of lead and other hazardous drinking-water lines on customers' property.
reasons.fiscal: The Legislative Fiscal Office says local spending may rise to the extent governments choose to fund this work.

label: Amendment 8
what: Prohibits a private entity that is a foreign adversary, or an agent of one (as defined by law, e.g. China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, Maduro-led Venezuela), from expropriating private property through eminent domain.
y: Foreign adversaries and their agents may not use expropriation in Louisiana.
n: Existing expropriation rules (public and necessary purpose, just compensation) remain without this specific ban.
fiscal: No fiscal note identified; no material fiscal effect expected beyond minimal ballot costs.
pro: Rep. Charles Owen (R, sponsor), Pelican Institute; passed House 100-0 and Senate 36-0

label: Amendment 9
t: Raise income cap for property-tax freeze to $150,000
what: Raises the income limit for the 'special assessment level' (which freezes a home's assessed value for homeowners 65+, disabled veterans rated 50%+, the permanently disabled, and certain military families) from $100,000 to $150,000 of adjusted gross income, indexed to inflation from 2028. Lost revenue must be absorbed by taxing bodies, not shifted to other taxpayers. Effective 2027.
y: More seniors, disabled people and veterans with incomes up to $150,000 can freeze their home's assessed value.
fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office: can only decrease local property-tax collections because a significant number of additional homes become eligible for the freeze from tax year 2027; the size cannot be determined because income data for owners isn't available. 422,344 properties already receive the special assessment; largest effect expected with 2028 reassessment. Possible indirect effect on state school (MFP) funding.
con: Pelican Institute (narrow carve-outs shift the tax burden)

reasons.fiscal: The Legislative Fiscal Office says it can only reduce local property-tax revenue as many more homes qualify for the assessment freeze, by an undetermined amount.

label: Amendment 10
t: Optional tax exemption for rehabilitated blighted property
what: Authorizes an optional local property-tax exemption for blighted or derelict property that has been rehabilitated. The legislature must define those terms and set the exemption's length, conditions and procedures. Applies from tax year 2027.
y: Local governments could exempt rehabilitated blighted property from property tax under rules the legislature sets.
fiscal: Legislative Fiscal Office: local revenue impact indeterminable; depends on how many parishes adopt it, how much rehabilitation it spurs and resulting value increases. Mainly forgone tax on the increased value after rehabilitation.
pro: Rep. Chance Henry (R, sponsor); passed House 80-12 and Senate 33-2

reasons.housing: Aims to encourage owners to rehabilitate blighted or derelict buildings.
reasons.fiscal: The Legislative Fiscal Office says localities would forgo some tax on the higher value of rehabilitated property, by an indeterminable amount.
